item.text: I’ll read those two brief files in full, create only `list.tsv`, then check the TSV’s formatting.

item.aggregated_output:
Read /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec3/luna/package.md. It holds image section 3 (Sıkma, öz ve ağzı kapalı şişe) of the frozen surah commentary of surah 103: the Arabic text of the ayat concerned, the Turkish
commentary written on them, the words/roots/branch labels recorded in the frozen surah commentary, and the
whole surah in Arabic. The selected commentary defines your scope; the other inputs supply context.

Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into
one quotation. Distinguish WLC's written/ketiv stream from qere and other readings; name another witness when
you rely on it. Discovery is memory-only: the later verifier will open the actual texts and check your claims.

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

Write one TSV row per distinct connection with exactly six tab-separated fields:

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

strength: strong, medium, weak. tradition: tevrat (Hebrew Bible and Jewish literature) or incil (New Testament and
Christian literature). kind: paralel, motif, karsi_anlati, soydas, yorum_gelenegi. ref: for the Hebrew Bible and
the New Testament an edition-qualified OSIS reference, one verse per row, no ranges
(WLC:Gen.22.2, WLC:Ps.1.3, SBLGNT:Matt.6.5; consecutive verses on their own rows).
Use Hebrew WLC numbering for Hebrew Bible candidates and SBLGNT numbering for New Testament candidates;
do not silently transfer English/KJV verse numbers. For other works give the work and its place as a reader
cites it (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 22:2;
Genesis Rabbah 56:1; Berakhot 60b; Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise 5:6; Protevangelium of James 8). basis: the words,
scene or motif that carries the link, in a few words. Strongest first. Keep distinct reasons or link kinds for
one passage in separate rows; exact repeated connections are unnecessary. Do not regrade an existing row.
The handoff groups references but preserves each distinct connection for an individual verdict.

Do not write a header row, rank numbers, Markdown, sections or prose outside TSV rows. Save the rows to
/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec3/luna/list.tsv. End nonempty files with a newline. Zero qualifying candidates means an explicitly created
empty file. The saved file, not the chat response, is the deliverable.

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

Asr kelimesinin en somut işi sıkmaktır: {ar:ضغط شيء حتى يتحلب, tr:dagtu şey'in hattâ yetehalleb, gloss:bir şeyi suyu akana kadar sıkmak, source:"ع ص ر,B002"}. Üzüm bir torbaya konur ve sıkılır: {ar:المعصار شيء كالمخلاة يجعل فيه العنب ويعصر, tr:el-mi'sâr, gloss:içine üzüm konup sıkılan yem torbası gibi bir şey, source:"ع ص ر,B002"}; akan şeyin adı usâredir {ar:العصارة ما تحلب من شيء تعصره, tr:el-usâra, gloss:sıktığın şeyden akan, source:"ع ص ر,B002"}. Araplar bu akan özü iyiliğin ve cömertliğin misali yapar: {ar:العرب تجعل العصارة والمعتصر مثلا للخير والعطاء, tr:el-arabu tec'alu'l-usârata mesalen li'l-hayr, gloss:Araplar usâreyi hayır ve bağış için misal yapar, source:"ع ص ر,B007"}. Aynı fiil insanın boğazında da işler: yemek boğazına takılan kişi suyu yudum yudum içerek onu geçirir: {ar:الاعتصار أن يغص الإنسان بالطعام فيعتصر بالماء, tr:el-i'tisâr en yagassa'l-insânu bi't-taâm, gloss:i'tisâr, insanın yemekle boğulup suyla onu geçirmesidir, source:"ع ص ر,B008"}. Susuzluktan kurumuş dil de "sıkılmış" diye anılır: {ar:المعصور اللسان اليابس عطشا, tr:el-ma'sûr, gloss:susuzluktan kurumuş dil, source:"ع ص ر,B014"}.

Surenin son kelimesi bu sahneyi kapatır. Sabır, bir ağaçtan sıkılan acı özün de adıdır: {ar:الصبر بكسر الباء عصارة شجرة, tr:es-sabir, gloss:sabir, bir ağacın usâresidir, source:"ص ب ر,B008"}, {ar:الصبر هذا الدواء المر, tr:es-sabru hâze'd-devâu'l-murr, gloss:sabır, bu acı ilaç, source:"ص ب ر,B008"}. Sabır kökü şişenin ağzını kapatan tıpayı {ar:الصبار صمام القارورة, tr:es-sibâr simâmu'l-kârûra, gloss:sibâr, şişenin tıpası, source:"ص ب ر,B018"} ve kabın kenarlarını {ar:أصبار الإناء نواحيه, tr:esbâru'l-inâ', gloss:kabın kenarları, source:"ص ب ر,B004"} de adlandırır. Böylece birinci ayetin kelimesi sıkmayı, üçüncü ayetin son kelimesi sıkılan özün kendisini ve onu tutan kabı anar: surenin başında baskı, sonunda o baskıdan çıkmış ve saklanmış acı bir ilaç vardır. Arada ikinci ayetin insanı durur; sıkılan kütle eksilir {ar:الخسر النقصان, tr:el-husru'n-nuksân, gloss:hüsr eksilmedir, source:"خ س ر,B001"}. Düz bir "sabırla birbirlerine tavsiye ettiler", sabrın bir sıkıştırmadan doğan, acı ama iyileştiren bir öz olduğunu duyurmaz.

Kur'an sıkmayı bir zindanda gösterir. Yusuf'la birlikte zindana giren iki gençten biri rüyasını anlatır: {ar:إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا, tr:innî erânî a'siru hamrâ, gloss:kendimi şarap için üzüm sıkarken görüyorum, source:12:36}. Aynı surede Yusuf kralın rüyasını yorarken yedi bolluk yılı, yedi darlık yılı sayar ve şöyle bitirir: {ar:ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ, tr:summe ye'tî min ba'di zâlike âmun fîhi yugâsu'n-nâsu ve fîhi ya'sirûn, gloss:sonra bir yıl gelir ki insanlar o yıl yardıma kavuşur ve o yıl sıkarlar, source:12:49}. Sıkmak burada darlığın bittiğinin işaretidir. Sabrın bir sıvı gibi kaptan dökülmesi de Kur'an'ın kendi dilindedir: Firavun'un sihirbazları tehdit karşısında {ar:رَبَّنَآ أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًۭا وَتَوَفَّنَا مُسْلِمِينَ, tr:rabbenâ efrig aleynâ sabran, gloss:Rabbimiz, üzerimize sabır boşalt ve bizi Müslüman olarak öldür, source:7:126} derler; Calût'un karşısına çıkanlar da aynı sözü söyler {source:2:250}. Ağzı mühürlü kap da Kur'an'da bir içeceğin değeridir: {ar:يُسْقَوْنَ مِن رَّحِيقٍۢ مَّخْتُومٍ, tr:yuskavne min rahîkın mahtûm, gloss:mühürlü saf bir içkiden içirilirler, source:83:25}.

/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec3/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.40.11	Commentary's 12:36 prison dream; grapes pressed into a cup	The imprisoned cupbearer dreams of taking grapes and pressing them into Pharaoh's cup, giving the commentary's prison grape-press scene in its own narrative setting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.32.19	Wine with no vent; new wineskins ready to burst	The commentary's cork holds squeezed liquid in a bottle; Elihu instead likens unspoken words to fermenting wine with no vent, so the same containment intensifies pressure toward rupture.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Song.4.12	Locked garden; sealed spring	The commentary's stopper keeps the bitter extract inside its vessel; the poem's sealed spring likewise contains a source, but presents closure as erotic exclusivity rather than medicine.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Jer.2.13	Living fountain; cracked cisterns	The commentary ends with a sealed bottle that retains its medicinal essence, whereas Jeremiah's chosen cisterns are cracked and cannot hold water, making failed containment a charge against Judah.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.15.25	Marah's bitter water and the wood	At Marah the people cannot drink bitter water until Moses throws a tree into it and it becomes sweet; this reverses the commentary's bitter tree extract, which remains bitter yet is named medicine.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.15.26	YHWH as healer	After the bitter-water episode, YHWH identifies himself as Israel's healer; this makes explicit the healing frame that the commentary gives to bitter sabr, though the remedy and bitterness work differently.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Lam.1.15	Judah trodden as grapes in a winepress	The lament says the Lord has trodden Judah like grapes in a press; the commentary's human squeezed into loss becomes a crushed people here, and the press yields devastation rather than a useful essence.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Isa.63.3	Winepress trodden in wrath; blood on garments	The divine speaker treads the press in anger and blood stains his clothing, a direct counter-image to the commentary's extracted juice as good and generous giving.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Joel.4.13	Ripe harvest; vats overflowing with wickedness	The harvest press overflows because the nations' wickedness is great; the shared pressing and yield imagery makes the commentary's beneficial extract read against a judgment harvest.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.20.7	Fig cake applied to a boil; recovery	Isaiah orders a fig cake laid on Hezekiah's boil and Hezekiah recovers; this gives a concrete plant-based remedy alongside the commentary's bitter tree extract called medicine.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Sirach 38:4	Medicines created from the earth	Sirach says the Lord made medicines from the earth and a sensible person does not reject them; it supplies a Jewish wisdom frame for the commentary's medicinal plant exudate as a beneficial natural substance.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.11.17	Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only	The Hebrew verb עצר closes the heavens so rain and yield cease; this restraint is the agricultural inverse of the commentary's squeezing that releases juice and, in its Yusuf comparison, marks relief after scarcity.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.2.7	Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only	Moses says Israel lacked nothing during the wilderness years; the cognate sense of lack gives a direct counter-reading to the commentary's human placed in decrease and loss.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.7.17	Commentary label root ء ن س; Hebrew אנש, regular sound correspondence and BDB Arabic-cognate note	Job asks what אנוש, a mortal human, is that God gives him such attention; it lends the commentary's generic human between pressure and loss a specific mortal and vulnerable register.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.7	Treasure in earthen vessels	Paul places treasure in fragile earthen vessels; this gives a close vessel image for the commentary's bottled essence, while locating the value in the vessel's contents rather than in a bitter remedy.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.8	Afflicted but not crushed	Paul says the community is pressed yet not crushed; this directly answers the commentary's image of the human as squeezed matter that decreases, with pressure failing to exhaust the people.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.9	Struck down but not destroyed	Paul distinguishes being struck down from being destroyed; this counters the commentary's equation of human pressure with decrease by describing survival after blows.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.5.3	Tribulation produces endurance	Paul says affliction produces endurance, which gives the commentary's squeezed, bitter sabr a developmental reading: pressure can generate the quality that sustains a person.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.5.5	God's love poured into hearts	Paul says God's love has been poured into believers' hearts; the commentary specifically notes Qur'anic patience poured over people, and this supplies a Christian liquid metaphor for an inward virtue, while naming love rather than patience.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.12.11	Painful discipline later yields peaceful fruit	Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit; this gives a precise interpretive bridge to the commentary's bitter medicine, whose discomfort is paired with healing benefit.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.12	Saints' endurance, God's commands, and faith in Jesus	The verse defines the saints by endurance, keeping God's commands, and faith in Jesus; this closely gathers patience, faithful action, and belief in the kind of people the commentary exempts from loss.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	Persistence in doing good and harvest in due season	Paul urges doing good without weariness because a harvest comes in due time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's righteous action and patience to an agricultural yield.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	Stirring one another to love and good works	The addressees are told to provoke one another toward love and good works; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal counsel and righteous deeds, though it specifies love rather than truth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.25	Encouraging one another	The assembly is to encourage one another as the day approaches; this supplies the reciprocal communal action behind the commentary's repeated mutual exhortation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.19	Turning a wanderer back from truth	James addresses fellow believers and says that whoever turns a brother back from wandering from the truth performs a communal corrective act like the commentary's mutual counsel in truth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.20	Saving a soul from death	James adds that bringing the wanderer back saves that person's soul from death; this makes the truth-directed mutual correction a rescue from loss, not merely instruction.
